title: How the lightsaber got its hum
hook: The lightsaber's hum is an old projector motor mixed with a TV's buzz.
peek: Star Wars sound designer Ben Burtt built the lightsaber from two accidents of everyday machinery: the idling motor of an old film projector and the buzz a television left on a microphone cable. Waving a microphone did the rest.
lede: When Ben Burtt started work on Star Wars in the 1970s, he had no idea what a laser sword should sound like. He found the answer in two pieces of old equipment. One was the steady hum of a film projector motor. The other was a buzz he caught by accident, and together they became one of cinema's most recognisable sounds.

bullets.text: At the University of Southern California, where he had studied film, Burtt knew the projection booth's old projectors. Their motors made a musical, steady hum as they idled, and he recorded it as the base of the sound.

Burtt walked past a television set carrying a microphone whose cable had lost its shielding. The cable picked up a buzz from the TV's picture tube. Mixed with the motor, it gave the hum its crackling edge.

To make the blades move, Burtt played the hum through a speaker and waved a microphone back and forth in front of it. The changing distance gave a natural Doppler swoosh, so each swing sounds different.
